title: The Windiest Corner in New York
voice_direction: Wry, unhurried American storyteller (Kurt). Land the hook plainly, a small smile on 'Everyone called it the Flatiron' and on 'twenty-three skidoo'; slow down for 'Etymologists aren't so sure', and give the last line a dry, settled finish.
narration: This building was blamed for lifting skirts. The Flatiron Building, finished in nineteen-oh-two where Broadway crosses Fifth Avenue. Officially, it was the Fuller Building. Everyone called it the Flatiron. At Twenty-third Street, its prow is about six and a half feet wide. When a north wind hit that point, it split and whipped down to the street. In October nineteen-oh-three, a film camera caught it: people on the corner, clutching their hats and skirts. An English visitor wrote that loafers gathered on the curb to watch, and police moved them on. That, the story goes, is where "twenty-three skidoo" comes from: police shooing men off Twenty-third Street. [pause] Etymologists aren't so sure. "Twenty-three," meaning "clear out," was already slang in eighteen ninety-nine, three years before the building opened. The wind was real. [pause] The slang just got there first.

instagram_caption:
The Flatiron Building was finished in 1902 on a wedge of land where Broadway crosses Fifth Avenue at 23rd Street. Officially it was the Fuller Building. Everyone called it the Flatiron.

Its prow is only about six and a half feet wide. When a north wind hit that point, it split around the building and whipped down to the sidewalk, and the corner got a reputation as the windiest in the city.

In October 1903 a Biograph cameraman filmed people at the foot of the Flatiron clutching their hats and skirts. An English visitor, Philip Burne-Jones, wrote in 1904 that loafers gathered on the curb to watch women's skirts blow about, and that police moved them on.

That, the story goes, is where "23 skidoo" comes from: police shooing men off 23rd Street.

Etymologists aren't so sure. "Twenty-three", meaning clear out, was already slang in 1899, three years before the building opened, and "skidoo" turns up in 1901. The wind was real. The slang just got there first.

Would you have said "23 skidoo"? 👇

facts.claim: The Flatiron (Fuller) Building, designed by D. H. Burnham & Co. and built by the George A. Fuller Co., was completed in 1902 (opened 1 October 1902) at Broadway, Fifth Avenue and 23rd Street; NYC landmark 20 September 1966 (LP-0219)
facts.source: NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission designation (LP-0219, 1966) via NYC LPC photo collection record; Wikipedia 'Flatiron Building'; Britannica 'Flatiron Building'

facts.claim: Its official name was the Fuller Building; the triangular plot was already called the 'flatiron' before construction (Chicago Daily Tribune, 27 May 1901: 'the new flatiron building to be erected at the junction of Broadway, Twenty-third Street, and Fifth avenue')
facts.source: Barry Popik, 'Flatiron District (Flatiron Building)', quoting Chicago Daily Tribune 27 May 1901 p. 5; History.com 'Flatiron Building'

facts.claim: The prow at the narrow north end is about 6.5 feet (2 m) wide
Wind from the north split around the building; downdrafts made the corner notoriously gusty
facts.source: Wikipedia 'Flatiron Building' (wind section); Library of Congress catalogue note for 'At the Foot of the Flatiron' (corner said by historians to be the windiest in the city)

facts.claim: In October 1903 Biograph cameraman A. E. Weed filmed pedestrians at the Flatiron's north corner on a very windy day, holding onto hats and skirts (copyright 2 November 1903; shot c. 26 October 1903)
facts.source: Library of Congress, 'At the foot of the Flatiron' (Paper Print Collection, item 00694378); Silent Era PSFL entry

facts.claim: Philip Burne-Jones (Dollars and Democracy, D. Appleton, New York, 1904) described loafers gathering on the curb at the corner to watch women's skirts blow about, and police 'moving on' anyone loitering there
facts.source: Columbia University Libraries record for Dollars and Democracy (1904); passage as reproduced by Edwardian Promenade and Rockwell Center (paraphrased in narration, not quoted)

facts.claim: The popular story says '23 skidoo' came from police shooing men away from the 23rd Street corner
facts.source: Library of Congress catalogue note for 'At the Foot of the Flatiron'; Museum of the City of New York ('some say')

facts.claim: The origin of '23 skidoo' is uncertain; 'twenty-three' as slang for leaving is in print by March 1899 (Morning Herald, Kentucky, 17 March 1899; George Ade 1899), 'skidoo' by 1901, and '23 skidoo' as a catchphrase from 1906, so the Flatiron cannot be the source of 'twenty-three'
facts.source: Barry Popik, 'Twenty-Three Skidoo (23rd Street myth)'; Wikipedia '23 skidoo' (citing the 1899 Morning Herald); Michelle Nevius, 'Postcard Thursday: Twenty-Three Skidoo'; FlatironNoMad Partnership 'origins are murky'

facts.claim: Alfred Stieglitz photographed the new Flatiron in a snowstorm in 1903 and published it as a photogravure in Camera Work
facts.source: Art Institute of Chicago, 'The Flatiron, 1903'; National Gallery of Art, 'The Flatiron' (key set); The Met 58.577.37

facts.claim: Edward Steichen photographed the Flatiron at dusk in 1904 (The Met 33.43.43 and 33.43.39, Alfred Stieglitz Collection; which Met URL is which print is unconfirmed)
facts.source: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 'The Flatiron' (Steichen, 1904)
